wal: punctuate direct speech accurately in my writing
tib: Speech punctuation helps the reader follow who is talking and makes dialogue feel purposeful and controlled.
isb: punctuating a prepared exchange and writing my own short dialogue between Varjak and a cat he meets.

title: Grammar Warm-Up
subtitle: Spot the correct version. Only one sentence in each pair is right.

cards.label: Pair A
lines: "You lost?" She said.
"You lost?" she said.
Which is correct?

cards.label: Pair B
lines: "I am looking for a dog," said Varjak.
"I am looking for a dog." said Varjak.
Which is correct?

cards.label: Pair C
lines: Said the cat "You have more courage than sense."
"You have more courage than sense," said the cat.
Which is correct?

title: Why does punctuation matter in dialogue?
lines: Here is a passage without any speech punctuation.
Try reading it aloud.
You lost said the cat.
No said Varjak. I am looking for a dog.
A dog said the cat. You have more courage than sense.
What is difficult?
Where does the spoken part end?
Who says which line?

title: Five rules for direct speech
left_lines: 1. Inverted commas around the spoken words.
2. Capital letter at the start of speech.
3. Punctuation before the closing inverted comma.
4. If a reporting clause follows, use a comma
(not a full stop) inside the inverted comma.

title: Punctuate together.
lines: Here is an unpunctuated exchange.
Let’s add the punctuation together.
What are you doing out here said the cat.
Looking for someone said Varjak.
Who asked the cat.
I don’t know yet said Varjak.
But I’ll know when I find them.
Use the five rules.
Remember: new speaker, new line.

title: Punctuate, then write your own.
lines: First: use your learning paper.
Punctuate the exchange between Varjak and Holly.
Use the five rules.
Then: write your own short exchange.
Varjak meets a cat for the first time.
Write three or four lines of dialogue.
At least one line must have
a reporting clause after the speech.
challenge: Add a sentence of description between two speech lines to show how a character feels without interrupting the dialogue.

q1: Which of the five rules do you find hardest to remember when you are writing quickly?
q2: How does starting a new line for each new speaker help the reader?
q3: What does the dialogue you wrote tell the reader about Varjak’s character?
